name: Freedom
lede: Freedom is a deep blue with a slight violet lean, a color name from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary that no book in our shelf discusses as a color.

sections.title: A dictionary name
sections.body: Freedom comes from Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930), which records the name as first used in 1919 and shows the color on plate 46, block A 12 [1]. The 1955 NBS Circular 553 cites it, and the ISCC-NBS system files this swatch under its block 179, called deep blue, about 5.6 units of color difference away [2]. Who coined the name, and for a dye, a fabric or a uniform, is undocumented in our sources, and our library lists it under fashion and textiles [1].

sections.title: What the books say about freedom
sections.body: None of the 29 books treats Freedom as a color [3][4]. They do tie the idea to two other colors, and neither is blue [3][4]. Pastoureau calls green the color of freedom in the modern West, and says national flags use it for liberty won from a ruling power, in Mexico, Bolivia, Bulgaria and Portugal [3]. He adds that green came close to being the color of the French Revolution in 1789 [3]. For red, he writes that the red cap was the sign of the freedom that people wanted when they refused to remain subjects and became citizens [4]. A deep blue called Freedom has borrowed a big word, and whether anyone meant it to carry that weight is undocumented in our sources [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is a dark blue in LCh terms: lightness 25.5, chroma 24 and hue angle 281, which puts it slightly toward violet [5]. Against white its contrast ratio is about 11 to 1 [5]. Its nearest named colors are [[dusky-blue]] and [[colonial]], both within about three units of color difference, then [[atlantis]] and [[liberty-blue]] a little further off [6]. The closest cut stone in our gem data is [[gem:lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]], a deep and less-flecked blue, at 3.8 units, with [[gem:spinel|blue spinel]] at 4.0 [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Freedom appears in 182 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 0.77 per cent, and is more common than 56 per cent of the named colors [7]. Counted by lightness rank inside each painting, which varnish cannot fake, it shows up in 82 works, most often as an accent (37 per cent of them) [7]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 1.6 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 3.4 times the baseline of the same museums [7].

The earliest match is a work of about 1350 by the Master of San Lucchese, 580 years before the name's first record [7]. That shows only that a dark blue in an aged photograph looks like this swatch. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [7].

openers: The color name Freedom is a 1919 dictionary entry for a deep blue, while the books link freedom with green and red.
A dark blue like this turns up in a work of about 1350, 580 years before the name existed.
